query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Inserting a thin, Ni-rich transition layer between HEA multilayers will enhance interface coherency, thereby mediating the creep mechanism transition from a primarily diffusion-controlled regime to one increasingly dominated by dislocation motion under high-temperature, sustained-stress conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayer coatings without an engineered transition layer, exhibiting ambiguous or diffusion-dominated creep behavior due to less-controlled interface coherency.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin, Ni-rich interlayer at the interfaces between HEA layers.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep conditions under sustained mechanical stress, where both diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated mechanisms are active.
generation.structural_mediator: A Ni-rich transition phase whose lattice parameters closely match those of adjacent HEA layers to form highly coherent interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The Ni-rich layer reduces lattice mismatch at the interfaces, lowers the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and motion, and thus facilitates a gradual shift from diffusion-controlled to dislocation-mediated creep as temperature and stress increase.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable shift in creep response with improved high-temperature performance, including lower creep strain rates and clearer evidence of dislocation activity in samples with the Ni-rich interlayer compared to controls.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the Ni-rich transition layer, which are expected to display a more diffusion-dominated creep mechanism.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected as long as the Ni-rich layer maintains interface coherency; at excessively high temperatures or prolonged exposure beyond a critical threshold, the interlayer may degrade, diminishing its mediating effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise shift in creep mechanism and the optimal thickness/composition of the Ni-rich layer required to achieve desired performance improvements remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA multilayers: one set with a carefully controlled, thin Ni-rich transition layer at the interfaces, and a control set without the interlayer. Subject both sets to high-temperature creep tests under identical sustained stress conditions.
measurements: Creep strain rates over time at various temperatures
Microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) to assess interface coherency and dislocation activity
Phase analysis to ensure the stability and integrity of the Ni-rich layer during testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Ni-rich interlayer do not exhibit a statistically significant shift in creep behavior (i.e., a clear transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated mechanisms) compared to control samples, or if the Ni-rich layer degrades interface coherency during testing, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

chosen.technique: magnetron sputtering for controlled multilayer deposition with in situ and ex situ characterization (HR-TEM, nanoindentation creep tests)
chosen.conditions: HEA multilayers with a deliberately inserted, ultra-thin Ni-rich coherent transition layer to modulate interface coherency, examined under variable high-temperature and stress conditions to capture the crossover from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the unexplained role of interface coherency by engineering and measuring its effect on the creep mechanism. By inserting a material (Ni-rich layer) with a lattice parameter that promotes coherence between HEA layers, the experiment isolates the impact of interface structure on the transition between creep mechanisms, making it a plausible and focused study using standard techniques in materials science.

decision.trend: Research in HEAs has advanced from bulk and monolithic systems—where processing methods (e.g., HPHT treatment, spark plasma sintering, selective laser melting) were used to tailor phase structures and interfacial coherency—to investigations that reveal how coherent interfaces can improve combined strength and ductility. In particular, the HPHT-treated eutectic HEA study demonstrated that minimizing lattice mismatch between adjacent phases (e.g., FCC and B2) yields highly coherent interfaces that trigger multiple deformation mechanisms. Although these studies achieved significant mechanical improvements through controlled interface structures, none have directly addressed how a tailored, coherent interface in multilayered HEA coatings might mediate the creep mechanism transition from diffusion‐controlled to dislocation‐controlled regimes.
decision.unsolved: The specific role of interface coherency in HEA multilayers—especially its dynamic influence on the creep behavior (transitioning from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated mechanisms at high temperatures under sustained stress)—remains unclear. There is a gap in understanding how an intentionally designed transition layer can bridge these mechanisms while preserving overall coating performance.
decision.lever: interface composition (introducing a thin, Ni-rich transition layer)
decision.why: Based on the trend of using process-controlled interface coherency to unlock sophisticated deformation mechanisms (as seen in HPHT-treated systems) and the niche requirement of clarifying creep mechanism transitions in HEA multilayers, the most plausible next step is to experimentally introduce a Ni-rich layer with lattice parameters closely matching the adjacent HEA layers. This lever is ideal because Ni-rich layers are known to form coherent interfaces in related systems, thus providing a well‐defined microstructural probe to delineate the influence of interface coherency on the relative roles of diffusion and dislocation creep during high-temperature operation.
